claim: RL safety guarantees of the tools McLean et al. propose do not transfer to deployed LLM agents, except a shield over properties of typed tool calls that sees every call, given a safe fallback; that shield uses nothing specific to RL.

The binding obstacles (conditions that fail in deployed agents and have not been shown to yield to scaling and function approximation) include irreversible actions (S6), hidden state (S4) and objectives, oversight and principals the agent's inputs can change (U1, U2 and U4; U3 in reported cases), in addition to the representation and model gaps McLean et al. name (S2, S3), which bind for properties of world state; that the guarantees need U1–U4 is our reading of the learning and optimality guarantees, not shown tool by tool.
Of the twelve works behind the tools McLean et al. offer, four state a guarantee about a safety constraint, four state another guarantee, and four state none.
The safety theorem of Wachi et al. 2023 needs a safe stop, defined as an emergency stop that resets the environment to the initial state (Assumption 3.3).
Altman 1999 CMDP constraints hold in expectation and do not bound the cost of one run; Satija et al. 2020 assume the MDP is ergodic for any policy.

Elelimy et al. say that the inability to revisit states makes ergodicity assumptions unrealistic in the real world; Lee 2025 (RSA) cannot prevent entering irreversible states before they are encoded, and a human resets the agent.
The shield and the Wachi certified safe set give safety guarantees that need little control of the learner (a filter or a changed input); only a post-posed shield is shown to wrap a frozen policy.
Mohammedalamen et al. 2025a need no task-specific safety information but need a finite, fully observable MDP with known transitions.
No LLM training setting fails more than one condition outright; in D-AGENT five of six stated conditions and three of four unstated conditions fail.
Seven of the eight works with a guarantee need in full a condition that fails in D-AGENT; the exception is shielding.

The cells that drive K09 and K10 are right: every D-AGENT cell and every training-column cell in 085_setting_conditions/cells.csv, and every full (checkmark) cell of a guaranteed work on a condition that fails in D-AGENT in 065_tool_conditions/cells.csv.

A shield over typed tool-call labels needs no model of world dynamics (the abstraction can be trivial) and keeps its guarantee for the properties its rules name; a property of world state needs a model (S2), which Alshiekh et al. call unavoidable when allowed actions depend on the environment state.

A certified safe set with a halting stop keeps the Wachi et al. safety theorem (Theorem 4.1) only given a safe halt (our hypothesis) and a delta-uncertainty quantifier for tool-call cost, for which we found no model; the proof of its near-optimality (Theorem 4.2) does not carry over, and whether it holds is open problem 2.
In the Replit incident, by the user's account, the agent said a rollback was impossible and the rollback then worked.

In the Terraform incident the agent ran a destroy with a state file that described production; no undo by the agent is reported, the snapshots were deleted, and the vendor restored the database after about 24 hours; the user saw the destroy announced and did not stop it.

McLean et al. concede that classical RL safety algorithms, which often rely on tabular representations, exact runtime shielding or known transition matrices, cannot be mapped one-to-one onto LLM backbones, and they frame this as a gap of scale.

McLean et al. name an inference-time shield over the action space, besides a constrained MDP, as a remedy for irreversible actions, and say the shield, as against KL regularisation, is what is missing from deployed agents.
The statements the paper attributes to McLean et al. (quotes, stances in the stance table, incident descriptions) match the text of McLean et al. 2026.

In the July 2026 evaluation incident, models left an isolated environment and entered third-party production systems; agents reasoned about the mechanism that scored them (metagaming, U3) and took goals from other agents (U1); the runs lacked deployed safeguards.
None of the cited tool papers reports an LLM-agent experiment; their evidence comes from grid worlds, MuJoCo, Safety Gym, Atari and real-robot goal-reaching.
The three open problems (authenticated objectives, safe exploration without reset, monitoring an agent that learns its monitor) are not solved by the cited prior work listed under 'Known'.
